a: Will they slip away for all their evil?
p: The Hebrew 'deliverance for them?' is odd. The Greek read 'for nothing'; many scholars read 'pay them back'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: for wickedness, escape for them?
readings.plain: Will they slip away for all their evil?

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ὑπὲρ τοῦ μηθενὸς σώσεις αὐτούς
readings.en: for nothing you will save them
readings.plain: For nothing will you save them;

readings.w: Proposed correction (BHS margin and many commentators): פַּלֶּס, 'weigh out, repay'
readings.en: for wickedness, repay them
readings.plain: For their evil, weigh out their payment.

why: The Hebrew can be read as an indignant question ("Shall they escape?", as in the KJV), so it is kept. The Greek seems to have read the word for "nothing" ('ayin) or "there is no escape"; the correction palles changes one letter and fits the next line.

a: Store my tears in your wineskin.
p: The Greek has 'You have put my tears before you', reading the Hebrew word for 'skin bottle' as 'in front of you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: put my tears in your skin bottle
readings.plain: Store my tears in your wineskin.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἔθου τὰ δάκρυά μου ἐνώπιόν σου
readings.orig: ἔθου τὰ δάκρυά μου ἐνώπιόν σου
readings.en: you have put my tears before you
readings.plain: You have put my tears in front of you.

why: The Hebrew wordplay between "my wandering" (nodi) and "your bottle" (nodekha) shows the Hebrew is original. The Greek probably read negdekha, "before you", a similar-looking word.

a: You gods, do you truly speak justice?
p: The Hebrew vowels give 'silence'; the same letters read 'gods' or 'mighty ones'. The Greek has neither.

readings.w: Revocalized ('elim), as most modern versions; compare 82:1
readings.en: Do you indeed, O gods, speak justice?
readings.plain: You gods, do you truly speak justice?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) as pointed (elem, 'silence'); KJV 'O congregation' (from a similar word)
readings.en: Do you indeed speak righteousness in silence?
readings.plain: Do you truly keep silent about justice?

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): εἰ ἀληθῶς ἄρα δικαιοσύνην λαλεῖτε
readings.en: If truly then you speak righteousness
readings.plain: If you truly speak justice,

why: This follows the same Hebrew letters with different vowels. "Silence" makes little sense with "speak", while "gods" (rulers or heavenly powers) fits the parallel "human beings" and Psalm 82. The vowels were added to the text centuries after it was written, so this is not a change of the consonantal text.
b: The KJV's "O congregation" comes from reading 'elem as related to 'alummah, a bundle or group.

a: My Strength, I will watch for you
p: The Leningrad Codex has 'his strength'. Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and 59:17 have 'my strength'.

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): τὸ κράτος μου; compare 59:17
readings.en: my strength, I will watch for you
readings.plain: My Strength, I will watch for you

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV '[Because of] his strength'
readings.en: his strength, I will watch for you
readings.plain: His strength! I will watch for you

why: The refrain returns in 59:17 as "my Strength" ('uzzi), and the letters vav (his) and yod (my) were easily confused. The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts have "my" here too. The Leningrad reading is hard to construe.

a: My God of loyal love will come to meet me.
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has 'his loyal love'; the spoken reading (Qere) has 'my God of loyal love'.

readings.w: Qere (the reading marked for reading aloud in the Masoretic Text); compare 59:17
readings.en: the God of my loyal love will meet me
readings.plain: My God of loyal love will come to meet me.

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants of the Leningrad Codex); Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ὁ θεός μου τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ προφθάσει με
readings.en: my God, his loyal love will meet me
readings.plain: My God: his loyal love will come to meet me.

why: The Qere matches the refrain in 59:17, "my God of loyal love". The Ketiv, supported by the Greek, is also good sense. The meaning is nearly the same.

a: answer me!
p: The written Hebrew has 'answer us', the spoken reading 'answer me'. The Greek and the written text of Psalm 108:6 have 'me'.

readings.w: Qere; Psalm 108:6 (Hebrew 108:7), written text with no Ketiv/Qere; Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἐπάκουσόν μου
readings.en: and answer me
readings.plain: answer me!

readings.w: Ketiv (Leningrad Codex consonants)
readings.en: and answer us
readings.plain: answer us!

why: The Qere, the written text of Psalm 108 and the Greek all agree on "me": the king or leader speaks for the people. "Us" suits the rest of the psalm, which says "we", and many modern versions follow it. The meaning is close either way.

a: All of you want to murder him,
t: You murder, or you will be murdered?
p: The Leningrad vowels say 'you will be murdered'; other Hebrew traditions and the Greek say 'you murder'.

readings.w: Ben Naphtali tradition and many Hebrew manuscripts (active תְּרַצְּחוּ); Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): φονεύετε πάντες
readings.en: you murder, all of you
readings.plain: All of you want to murder him,

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (passive תְּרָצְּחוּ); KJV 'ye shall be slain all of you'
readings.en: you will be murdered, all of you
readings.plain: All of you will be murdered,

why: The question "How long will you storm against one man?" leads naturally to the attackers' aim, murder, and the Greek agrees. The passive, a warning to the attackers, is the Leningrad pointing and is possible. The consonants are the same.

a: A psalm of David. A song.
t: A longer title in the Greek
p: The Greek adds that this was a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, from the time of the exile.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: A psalm of David. A song.
readings.plain: A psalm of David. A song.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ᾠδή Ιερεμιου καὶ Ιεζεκιηλ ἐκ τοῦ λόγου τῆς παροικίας
readings.orig: ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαυιδ ᾠδή Ιερεμιου καὶ Ιεζεκιηλ ἐκ τοῦ λόγου τῆς παροικίας ὅτε ἔμελλον ἐκπορεύεσθαι
readings.en: A psalm of David. A song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, from the account of the exile, when they were about to go out.
readings.plain: A psalm of David. A song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, from the story of the exile, when they were about to go out.

why: The Greek title is a later reader's link, like the Greek titles of Psalms 71 and 96–99. No Hebrew witness has it. It shows how Jews in the Greek-speaking world read the psalm: as a prayer for the return from exile.

a: silence is praise
p: The Hebrew 'silence (is) praise'; the Greek 'a hymn is fitting'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew (tibi silens laus, as usually cited)
readings.en: to you silence is praise
readings.plain: silence is praise

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): σοὶ πρέπει ὕμνος
readings.en: to you a hymn is fitting
readings.plain: praise is fitting

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading and makes good sense (compare 62:1). The Greek probably read domiyyah or dommiyah, "fitting, like", from damah. Many modern versions follow the Greek ("Praise is due to you").

a: A song. A psalm.
p: The Greek title adds 'of resurrection' (anastaseōs).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: A song. A psalm.
readings.plain: A song. A psalm.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ᾠδὴ ψαλμοῦ ἀναστάσεως
readings.en: A song of a psalm, of resurrection
readings.plain: A song of a psalm, of resurrection.

why: No Hebrew witness has the addition. It may reflect the psalm's line "He set our souls in life" (66:9) or its use at a festival. Christians later sang it at Easter.

a: the one who rides through the desert plains
t: Deserts, the west, or the clouds?
p: The Hebrew has 'the deserts'; the Greek read 'the west'; a Canaanite title suggests 'the clouds'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV 'him that rideth upon the heavens' (by interpretation)
readings.en: for the rider in the desert plains
readings.plain: the one who rides through the desert plains

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): τῷ ἐπιβεβηκότι ἐπὶ δυσμῶν
readings.en: for the one who has mounted upon the west (or the sunsets)
readings.plain: the one who rides over the west

readings.w: Proposed reading from the Ugaritic title of Baal, rkb 'rpt (בָּעֲרָפוֹת); many modern versions
readings.en: for the rider on the clouds
readings.plain: the one who rides on the clouds

why: The Hebrew word means dry plains and fits God's march through the wasteland in 68:7. The "clouds" reading needs a change of letter, or a rare meaning of the word; it is attractive because of 68:33 and Deuteronomy 33:26, but it is not in any manuscript. The Greek's "west" reads the word as 'erev, "evening".

a: Sinai is in the holy place.
t: Sinai in the holy place, or came from Sinai?
p: The Hebrew 'the Lord among them, Sinai in holiness'. A small change gives 'the Lord came from Sinai into the holy place'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἐν Σινα ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ
readings.en: the Lord among them, Sinai in the holy place
readings.plain: Sinai is in the holy place.

readings.w: Proposed reading (dividing the letters as בָּא מִסִּינַי), many modern versions
readings.en: the Lord came from Sinai into the holy place
readings.plain: He came from Sinai into the holy place.

why: The Hebrew and the Greek agree, and the line makes sense as it stands: God's Sinai presence now dwells in the sanctuary. The correction, which echoes Deuteronomy 33:2, changes the way the letters are divided and adds one letter; no manuscript has it.

a: You took gifts among humans,
p: The Hebrew and Greek say 'you took gifts'. The Targum, the Syriac and Ephesians 4:8 say 'you gave gifts'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἔλαβες δόματα ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ
readings.en: you took gifts among humans
readings.plain: You took gifts among humans,

readings.w: Targum of Psalms ('you gave them as gifts to the sons of men'); Syriac Peshitta (as usually reported); Ephesians 4:8 (ἔδωκεν δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις)
readings.en: he gave gifts to people
readings.plain: You gave gifts to humans,

why: The Hebrew and the Greek agree on "took", which fits a victor receiving tribute. Paul's "gave" matches the Targum's interpretation, which shows that he was reading the verse in a way known in Jewish tradition, not inventing a new text. The site follows the Hebrew; the variant shows the reading Paul used.
b: The Targum and the Syriac were not checked directly; they are given as reported in Stec's translation of the Targum and in the commentaries.

a: so that your foot may stamp in blood,
p: The Hebrew 'that your foot may crush (in) blood'; the Greek 'be dipped in blood', from a word one letter different.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (תִּמְחַץ)
readings.en: so that your foot may crush (or wade) in blood
readings.plain: so that your foot may stamp in blood,

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ὅπως ἂν βαφῇ ὁ πούς σου ἐν αἵματι; compare 58:10 (תִּרְחַץ)
readings.orig: ὅπως ἂν βαφῇ ὁ πούς σου ἐν αἵματι
readings.en: so that your foot may be dipped in blood
readings.plain: so that your foot may be bathed in blood,

why: The Hebrew is hard but can mean stamping through blood. The Greek and the parallel in 58:10 suggest tirchats, "bathe", which many modern versions adopt. The sense is the same: total victory.

a: Your God has ordered your strength.
t: Your God has ordered, or Command, God?
p: The Hebrew has 'your God has ordered your strength'; the Greek has 'Command, God, your strength'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (צִוָּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ)
readings.en: your God has commanded your strength
readings.plain: Your God has ordered your strength.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἔντειλαι, ὁ θεός, τῇ δυνάμει σου; many modern versions (revocalized צַוֵּה אֱלֹהִים)
readings.en: command, God, your strength
readings.plain: Command your strength, God.

why: The consonants allow both. The Hebrew as written speaks to Israel about what God has done; the Greek reading makes the line a prayer, matching the next line, "Be strong, God". The KJV follows the Hebrew and many modern versions follow the Greek. The sense is close: God's strength musters his people.

a: and for their friends a snare.
t: For their friends, or for retribution?
p: The Hebrew vowels give 'for those at peace (allies)'; the Greek and Romans 11:9 read 'for retribution'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (לִשְׁלוֹמִים)
readings.en: and for those at peace, a snare
readings.plain: and for their friends a snare.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org) (εἰς ἀνταπόδοσιν καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον, 'for retribution and for a stumbling block'); Romans 11:9
readings.en: and for retribution and a stumbling block
readings.plain: and a payback and a snare.

why: The consonants allow both: shelomim "those at peace, friends" (or "peace offerings") and shillumim "payment, retribution". The site keeps the Masoretic vowels, which make a fair parallel with "their table": the meal shared with friends becomes the trap. Paul quotes the Greek wording in Romans 11:9.

a: and they gossip about the hurt of the ones you wounded.
t: Tell of the pain, or add to it?
p: The Hebrew 'they recount the pain'; the Greek 'they added to the pain of your wounded'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (יְסַפֵּרוּ)
readings.en: and they tell of the pain of your wounded
readings.plain: and they gossip about the hurt of the ones you wounded.

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἐπὶ τὸ ἄλγος τῶν τραυματιῶν σου προσέθηκαν; Syriac (as reported)
readings.orig: ἐπὶ τὸ ἄλγος τῶν τραυματιῶν σου προσέθηκαν
readings.en: they added to the pain of your wounded
readings.plain: and they add to the hurt of the ones you wounded.

why: The Hebrew makes sense: the enemies spread talk about the sufferer's pain. The Greek probably read yosifu, "they add", which fits 69:27 ("Add guilt to their guilt") and is followed by many modern versions. The Leningrad reading is kept.

a: Be a rock to live in for me,
t: A rock to live in, or a rock of refuge?
p: The Leningrad Codex has 'rock of dwelling'; 31:2, some manuscripts and the Greek have 'rock of refuge'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (מָעוֹן)
readings.en: be to me a rock of dwelling
readings.plain: Be a rock to live in for me,

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts and 31:2 (מָעוֹז); Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): γενοῦ μοι εἰς θεὸν ὑπερασπιστὴν (καὶ εἰς τόπον ὀχυρόν)
readings.en: be to me a rock of refuge (Greek: a protecting God and a strong place)
readings.plain: Be a rock of refuge for me,

why: Both readings make good sense, and the Leningrad reading is supported by 90:1 and 91:9, where God is a "dwelling" (ma'on). The other reading may be an echo of 31:2.

a: You have made me see many troubles and disasters,
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has 'us' in this verse; the spoken reading (Qere) and the Greek have 'me'.

readings.w: Qere; Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ὅσας ἔδειξάς μοι θλίψεις
readings.en: you have made me see ... you will make me live
readings.plain: You have made me see many troubles and disasters,

readings.w: Ketiv (Leningrad Codex consonants)
readings.en: you have made us see ... you will make us live
readings.plain: You have made us see many troubles and disasters,

why: The rest of the psalm is spoken by one person, and the Qere and the Greek agree. The Ketiv "us" may show that the psalm was also prayed by the community. Both changes in the verse go together.

a: May they fear you as long as the sun lasts,
t: They will fear you, or he will live long?
p: The Hebrew 'may they fear you'; the Greek 'may he continue with the sun', from a different verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: may they fear you with the sun
readings.plain: May they fear you as long as the sun lasts,

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): καὶ συμπαραμενεῖ τῷ ἡλίῳ (reading וְיַאֲרִיךְ, 'and may he prolong')
readings.en: and he will continue with the sun
readings.plain: May he live on as long as the sun lasts,

why: The Hebrew is kept, though the sudden "you" (God) is surprising in a psalm about the king. The Greek reading keeps the subject on the king and matches 72:17 and 61:6, and many modern versions follow it. Both are old; the Hebrew is the harder reading.

a: Let the righteous bloom in his days,
p: The Leningrad Codex has 'the righteous'; some Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and the Syriac have 'righteousness'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (צַדִּיק)
readings.en: in his days may the righteous flourish
readings.plain: Let the righteous bloom in his days,

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): ἀνατελεῖ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτοῦ δικαιοσύνη; Syriac (as reported); Jerome's Gallican Psalter, made from the Greek
readings.orig: ἀνατελεῖ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτοῦ δικαιοσύνη
readings.en: righteousness will dawn in his days
readings.plain: Let righteousness bloom in his days,

why: Both are good sense. "Righteousness" matches "peace" in the second line and 72:3, so it may be original; "the righteous" matches the psalm's concern for people. The Leningrad reading is kept.

a: May people bless themselves by him;
t: A longer blessing in the Greek
p: The Greek has 'and all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him', closer to Genesis 12:3 and 28:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and may they bless themselves by him
readings.plain: May people bless themselves by him;

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek, Rahlfs; checked on blueletterbible.org): καὶ εὐλογηθήσονται ἐν αὐτῷ πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς
readings.orig: καὶ εὐλογηθήσονται ἐν αὐτῷ πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: and all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him
readings.plain: May all the clans of the earth be blessed in him;

why: The Hebrew line is short and has no subject, so the Greek may preserve words that dropped out ("all the clans of the earth", as in Genesis 12:3 and 28:14) or may have filled the gap from Genesis. The site keeps the Hebrew and shows the fuller reading here.
